Two solve a system of linear equations, one by systematic cancelling (Gauss elimination) and one by repeated guessing that improves itself (Gauss–Seidel); the third, the simplex method, finds the best value of a linear quantity subject to linear restrictions.

Rounding error accumulates in direct methods, and ill-conditioned systems magnify small errors. Gauss elimination solves a system in a fixed number of steps, whereas Gauss-Seidel improves a guess repeatedly and converges for diagonally dominant systems.

Linear programming finds the best value (maximum profit or minimum cost) of a linear objective function subject to linear constraints (inequalities). A factory in Hetauda planning its products with limited machine hours is a typical application.
